Mutators notify one fine-grained channel — 'targets' (:57), 'result' (:74), 'leaderboard' (:83), 'province' (:92), 'performance' (:101). All 16 panels implement the SAME binding contract verbatim: guard `if (!state || typeof state.subscribe !== 'function') return () => {}`, then `state.subscribe((snapshot, channel) => { if (channel !== '<x>' && channel !== 'all') return; const payload = snapshot.get<X>(); if (!payload) return; render(payload); })` — armyPanel:189, bonusPanel:90, expeditionPanel:337, gbDonationPanel:993, gbgPanel:894, greatBuildingsPanel:527, incidentsPanel:250, investedPanel:185, outpostPanel:150, quantumPanel:391, resourcePanel:367, rewardRenderBinding:22, socialPanel:288+313, startupPanel:67+85, treasuryPanel:551. TWO properties matter. (1) Error containment: notify() wraps EACH subscriber call in try/catch and logs 'Reactive subscriber failed' with the channel and message (:42-53), so a throwing panel cannot break the state mutator or the other subscribers — the failure is contained at the UI boundary by design. (2) The parameter named `snapshot` is NOT a snapshot: notify passes `this` (:45), the live mutable state object, and getters like getTargets() return the live field. A subscriber retaining that reference observes later mutations, so the name misleads and any 'immutable snapshot' assumption is wrong. Panels are additionally fail-soft: an unwired panel renders nothing rather than throwing. msg/StartupService.js:862 consumes the same contract on metadataStore but debounces it, guarding re-entrancy with a metadataRenderTimer.

subject: src/js/protocol/xhrInterceptor.js:129-152 (dispatchWsText)
verdict: The origin gate is tautologically satisfied for all WebSocket traffic, and this is a data-integrity bug with a security dimension that is SUBSUMED by the project's existing baseline. Verified at xhrInterceptor.js:145: dispatchWsText posts `url: window.location.origin + '/game/json?source=ws'` — a literal concatenation. attachWsListener(ws) (:154) receives the socket but never reads ws.url, so the real destination is discarded and EVERY WebSocket the page opens, to ANY host, is relabelled as a same-origin /game/json request. That synthesized URL then passes evaluateRequestOrigin at networkListener.js:460 unconditionally, so intakePolicy.js's careful https/suffix/path checks provide zero discrimination here. The body filter is only `rawData.startsWith('[') || startsWith('{')` (:131-132), and the frame is dispatched to MessageDispatcher as a normal game JSON-RPC response, so any service that mutates state on a well-formed payload will act on it. ADJUDICATION — this is not a new privilege escalation: SECURITY.md already documents that MAIN-world messages are page-spoofable, and contentBridge.js:46 only checks `event.source === window && event.origin === window.location.origin`, which any script running in the page satisfies, so an attacker who can run script there could already post a synthetic FOE_INFO_XHR with a genuine-looking URL. What WS synthesis adds is that it needs NO attacker: a page that legitimately opens a third-party WebSocket (analytics, chat, ads) has that traffic silently injected into the extension's state pipeline as trusted game traffic. The real-WS-destination data-fidelity loss is a secondary but permanent diagnostic blind spot. Fix shape: carry the real ws.url through dispatchWsText and let the existing origin gate decide, rather than asserting an origin.
question: Does the WebSocket branch of the MAIN-world interceptor preserve the passive-observation and origin-gate invariants?

subject: .gitattributes, forge-hammer/.gitignore, forge-hammer/.gitattributes
verdict: Caveat 1 (churn) was largely a measurement error on my part and is now resolved. I had claimed 'roughly 8 MiB of churn per refresh'; that was the WORKING-TREE size, not the git cost. Measured empirically in throwaway repos over 11 commits: graph.json adds ~304 KiB per AST refresh and graph.html ~264 KiB, because both compress to ~6% (4.4 MiB -> 248 KiB gzipped). graph.json is pretty-printed at 140k lines with a 413-char max line, so it is also diffable if you ever want to. So both stay tracked. The REAL risk was not size but merge conflicts on a 140k-line JSON, and that is now solved properly rather than by dropping files: merge.graphify.driver was ALREADY in git config, but there was no .gitattributes, so git never invoked it — graphify hook status reported 'partially registered (git config set, .gitattributes line missing)'. Adding `graphify-out/graph.json -diff merge=graphify` completes it; both repos now report 'merge driver: registered' and check-attr confirms merge=graphify, diff=unset. End-to-end verified in a scratch repo: two branches each adding a node to graph.json merged CLEAN, both nodes survived, zero conflict entries. `-diff` also keeps git from attempting a 140k-line textual diff. Deliberately NOT marked -diff: memory/, reflections/ and findings/, because reviewing how a verdict changed is the point of tracking them. Deliberately did NOT run `graphify hook install` in FoE-Info-Extension: it adds a post-commit hook that rebuilds the graph on every commit, which on a 490-file/4.4 MiB graph is a real per-commit cost. Caveat 2 (siblings) resolved by inspection and mostly dissolved — metadata-store is NOT a git repository at all (`fatal: not a git repository`) and its graph.json alone is 283 MiB, so there is nothing to do and tracking it would be absurd; FoE-Info-Extension-original's graphify-out/ is EMPTY (0 entries), also nothing to do; only forge-hammer needed the change, and its graph is 484 KiB, not 4.4 MiB. forge-hammer got the identical selective pattern plus the .gitattributes, verified: 9 files trackable, 7 spot-checked local paths still ignored, driver registered. forge-hammer has no prettier config or format script, so unlike this repo it needs no .prettierignore. Its post-commit hook ALREADY anticipates tracked output — it exits early when only graphify-out/ paths changed, commented 'avoids rebuild loop when graph outputs are tracked in git' — and it deliberately does not stage, so the rebuilt graph surfaces as a follow-up amend rather than a phantom auto-commit. `npm run verify` green after the .gitattributes addition: 1750 tests, 0 fail, webpack compiled.

subject: .husky/post-commit, .husky/post-checkout, graphify hook install
verdict: It attaches to HUSKY, not .git/hooks, and that distinction matters. `graphify hook install` wrote .husky/post-commit (285 lines) and .husky/post-checkout (13k) — both NEW files; it did not touch the existing .husky/pre-commit or .husky/pre-push, so the lint-staged/typecheck and full-verify gates are intact. Dispatch is: git -> .husky/_/post-commit (shim) -> .husky/_/h -> resolves dirname(dirname($0))/post-commit = .husky/post-commit -> `sh -e`. That resolution is why installing into .husky/ works here even though .git/hooks/ is empty: wiring comes from `core.hooksPath=.husky/_` (repo-local, set by the `prepare: husky` script, husky ^9.1.7). Verified `graphify hook status` now reports post-commit: installed, post-checkout: installed, merge driver: registered. `graphify hook install` is also non-destructive about the merge driver — it reported 'already registered' rather than rewriting it. THREE behaviours worth knowing. (1) The rebuild is DETACHED: the hook prints '[graphify hook] launching background rebuild' and returns in 0s, so a commit is never blocked; the graph lands a moment later as an unstaged modification to amend. (2) It deliberately exits in a git worktree, because --git-dir is .git/worktrees/<name> while --git-common-dir is .git and they differ — so the hook will not clobber the main checkout's graph. I hit this while testing and it is correct behaviour, not a failure. (3) graph.json is written ATOMICALLY: polling it 535 times across a full rebuild produced 0 corrupt reads, so a concurrent reader or a `git add` can never capture a partial file. An earlier KeyError observed mid-rebuild was my own script reading an 'edges' key when the schema uses 'links', not evidence of corruption. Caveat not solved: the post-commit rebuild reports 'community set changed since labeling (342 saved labels, 342 communities now; renamed 102 community(ies) by their hub)', meaning community NAMES degrade toward hub-derived labels after AST-only refreshes; restoring them needs `graphify label` (tier 3, LLM).
question: What does 'graphify hook install' actually attach to in this repo, and does it fire?

verdict: No — and the premise is worth correcting, because acting on it would have reproduced the defect rather than fixed it. MEASUREMENT FIRST. All four git-backed graphs were already at their repository's HEAD via built_at_commit, and `find -newer graph.json` found ZERO source files newer than the graph in every one of them. So nothing was stale by commit or by source. Deleting and rebuilding bought freshness they already had. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG is the LABEL TIER. An unlabeled graph names each community after its highest-degree file, so a community query returns a filename as though it were a topic. Measured before the fix: forge-hammer 24 of 125 communities filename-derived, LoW-Tool 27 of 189, foe-info-original 12 of 112 — every one of them freshly extracted and current against its source. forge-hammer was answering 'Charting' questions with 'jquery.tabslet.min.js', 'lit-html.bundle.min.js' and '_main.js'. Only this repo had ever been labeled. THE DECISIVE POINT: re-extracting a current AST REPRODUCES filename names, which is why the two graphs the owner had just rebuilt were still degraded. A rebuild is not a substitute for labeling. `graphify.sh <target> label` relabels without re-extracting, so it is both the correct repair and the cheap one (~100s per target). Ran it on forge-hammer, foe-info-original and low-tool: all four code graphs now 0 filename-derived, and forge-hammer's community names became Charting, Chart Layout, Axis Calculation, Map Building, React Nodes. metadata has no communities at all (0 of 5499 nodes carry a community id — it is built from entity JSON by build-metadata-graph.mjs, not clustered), so it is n/a rather than unlabeled. SECOND HALF — the derived exports. The owner asked whether the wiki/, obsidian/, graph.svg, graph.html, GRAPH_TREE.html, *-callflow.html, dated snapshot directories and cache/ were needed. They are not: graph.json is the only artifact a query reads and GRAPH_REPORT.md the only human-facing summary. The reason they existed is that graphify.sh ran an unconditional `$RUNNER export wiki` at the end of EVERY ast/update/reindex/label branch, which is 26M of obsidian/ plus 1.7M of wiki/ in metadata-store alone, none of it read. Fixed at the source: a --export flag parsed out of the argument list plus a maybe_export helper, so all five branches are opt-in and --export never reaches graphify itself. Deleted the stale exports from forge-hammer (11M -> 2.8M) and metadata-store (335M -> 283M), verified by md5 that graph.json was byte-identical in both. Kept findings/, memory/, reflections/, manifest.json and GRAPH_REPORT.md. PROPAGATED, since the owner's point was that the generators should reflect this: the graphify skill gained a 'label tier is not optional' section with a one-liner that counts filename-derived communities, and a 'derived exports are opt-in' section; maintain-graph-knowledge gained a 'Know Which Graph You Are Reading' section stating that a missing wiki is expected and never evidence of a broken graph, and that structural queries are unaffected by label decay while community NAMES are; the AGENTS.md graph catalog gained a Labeled column and had its stale 'absent — deliberately removed' row corrected; both tier tables stopped claiming exports are included; .gitignore in this repo and forge-hammer now ignore obsidian/, graph.svg, GRAPH_TREE.html and *-callflow.html so running export once cannot stage tens of megabytes. Verified by `git add -An` that forge-hammer would track exactly graph.json, graph.html, GRAPH_REPORT.md, memory/, reflections/ and findings/. RESULT: 1765 tests pass, 0 fail, webpack compiled, audit:refs 0 findings, all five graphs labeled and current. The general lesson: 'stale' and 'low quality' are different diagnoses with the same symptom, and freshness is the one that is cheap to check and easy to mistake for the other.

It stays closed source and re-syncs from this repo, keeping its guild features (GenClub, team sniping) as an ADDITIVE MODULE on top. The two are complementary, not competing. Prior framing in docs/TODO.md described the low-tool graph target as reinstated 'because the owner wants the cross-repo graphs queryable for the refactor', i.e. a convenience; that is now recorded as a standing architecture instead. subject: LoW-Tool src/js/msg/GreatBuildingsService.js:1028-1074 (addGB / copyText / GBlist / clearGBlist)
verdict: CORRECTION to the previous row, which said it was dead. It is not dead — it is SHADOWED, and the distinction changes what the sync must do. I asserted 'no caller anywhere in src/' from a grep of the symbol GBlist, which was the wrong search: GBlist is only the backing array, and the entry points are addGB (:1028) and copyText (:1051). Searching those by name across the whole fork, not just src/js, shows what actually happens. There are TWO GreatBuildingsService modules: the core one at src/js/msg/ and a second at src/extras/msg/. Both build a donation clipboard payload, and both name a local `copyText` — but the core's is a FUNCTION DECLARATION at :1051 while extras' is a LOCAL VAR at :154. Where extras' module is in scope, the local var shadows the core function, so the core copyText() is unreachable from those call sites; and addGB() has no caller in either module, so GBlist is only ever appended by a function nothing invokes. The live clipboard behaviour is extras' own copyText, which builds the same <div id='copyText'> markup and binds copy.DonationCopy at :441. So the feature is genuinely still in the product — it just lives in src/extras/ where it belongs, and the core copy is a leftover from BEFORE the extras module was split out. That is a better outcome for the sync than 'dead code': it means the desired end state (core replaced wholesale from upstream, extras preserved) loses nothing, and the two core files need no hand-merge at all. METHOD NOTE, because it caused the error: I claimed I 'could not see' anything outside src/ and that a grep could not settle it. That was wrong on both counts — the whole fork is readable, and a symbol search for the ARRAY rather than for the two FUNCTIONS is what produced the false negative. The two greps that appeared to return nothing were also misleading: piping through `cut -c1-95` truncated the leading path off every line, so the output was whitespace. Trusting that reading would have produced a second wrong conclusion. When a search returns nothing unexpected, re-run it without the formatting pipeline before believing it.

verdict: The cost is in src/extras/, and the measurement is much larger than the 3-file core diff suggested. src/extras/ is 6,266 lines across 11 files — 55% the size of the fork's entire 11,340-line core — and it splits cleanly into two groups by whether a core counterpart exists. SHADOWING (8 files, ~4,099 lines): msg/GreatBuildingsService.js (892 lines, ~73% identical to its core counterpart), msg/OtherPlayerService.js (1,071, ~64%), msg/ConversationService.js (160, ~54%), plus devtools.js, index.js, options.js, popup.js, vars/showOptions.js. The number that actually predicts future maintenance is the 4,099 shadowed lines, because that is the surface where a core change must be applied twice with nothing enforcing it. This is the mechanical explanation for what the owner described as 'duplicate code that's not actively synced': the msg/ shadowing files are near-verbatim module copies (54-73% identical), so they carry all the cost and none of the uniqueness, while the 3 genuinely additive files carry all the uniqueness and none of the cost. Copying src/js/ forward from upstream is necessary but NOT sufficient: it leaves those 3 msg/ copies just as stale as the core they shadow, so the fork would still need a manual sync on the next upstream change to GreatBuildingsService, OtherPlayerService or ConversationService. The step that actually ends the maintenance problem is converting each copy into an override — diff it against its new upstream counterpart, keep only the delta that is genuinely LoW behaviour, delete the rest. That step is also independently verifiable, because the shadowing file and its upstream counterpart can be diffed directly. Note the dependency direction is already correct and should be preserved: extras/ imports only from ../js/, never the reverse, so overriding does not require the core to know about extras. The owner's report that they could not maintain it is consistent with this structure rather than evidence of a learning gap — with 73% duplication and no enforcement, the only way to keep the fork in step was to notice every upstream change by hand.

Line counts, original -> fork core -> extras copy -> UPSTREAM TODAY: GreatBuildingsService 1,025 -> 1,074 -> 892 -> 547; OtherPlayerService 1,537 -> 1,537 -> 1,071 -> 466; ConversationService 169 -> 169 -> 160 -> 339. The copies sit near their ANCESTOR's size, not upstream's, and src/js/msg/ grew from 11 services to 32 with the Great Building domain decomposed into GbDonationService, InvestedService and GbgSignalService. A copy shadowing a 1,537-line monolith cannot be diffed onto a 466-line module plus three new siblings. This also corrects the owner's own mental model, gently: the extras copies are not 'core plus extra stuff on top' any more, they are STALE SNAPSHOTS. Three measurements establish it. (1) They define ZERO symbols of their own — a module that adds features normally introduces new top-level functions, and these introduce none. (2) They DROP 14 symbols the core has, including all nine blueAttack*/blueDefense*/redAttack* GBG functions. verdict: No — and my previous row called this a silent defect, which was WRONG. It is by design and it is our usage error. reflect.py:387-412 scores graph NODES per memory (source_nodes, time-decayed, useful=+1 / dead_end|corrected=-1) and renders corrections at :483 as '"<question>" -> <correction>'. subject: BonusService.getBonuses
verdict: Keep it deferred, and the reason is now concrete rather than an evidence gap. The captured payload is the PERSISTENT city-wide list - three entries, all with `value` and a *Bonus class: recruitment_acceleration 40, construction_rebate 25, daily_strategypoint 20. The handled getLimitedBonuses is the opposite: entity-scoped and temporary (LimitedBonusFromEntity, isActive, entityId, factor). So they are different data with exactly one overlapping type, daily_strategypoint - and getLimitedBonuses already accumulates that into City.ForgePoints through a base+delta accumulator. Wiring getBonuses into the same handler would re-add 20 FP on every response and corrupt the total. Deferred until a feature needs persistent bonuses, and then it needs its own handler, not this one.
